entities.name: Decisions
entities.tagline: A call that set what the work would be — what to build, in what order and what to stop.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
An achievement whose claim is the choice itself: a ranking agreed, a roadmap rewritten, a feature retired, a direction someone had to be talked into. What makes it this kind is that somebody else could have carried it out once the call was made.

Carrying it out is Delivery, even where the same person did both, and what came of it is Results. A bullet that decided and built in one sentence is filed by whichever half the entry would be poorer without.

entities.name: Delivery
entities.tagline: Something built, changed or taken apart, and in the hands of the people it was for.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
An achievement whose claim is the work done: a system replaced, a service split, a migration run, a process put in place. It names what changed and who has it now.

Choosing what to build is Decisions. What the change turned out to be worth — a measured effect, a finding, an outcome still owed — is Results, and it goes there even where one sentence could carry both.

entities.name: Results
entities.tagline: What came of the work — an effect measured, a finding established or an outcome still owed.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
An achievement whose claim is the consequence rather than the act: what changed because the work was done, what it turned out to show, and what it has not delivered yet. An entry's honest unfinished business is this kind, because it is an outcome like any other.

The work that produced the result is Delivery, and the call that aimed it is Decisions. The result is filed apart from both, so a reader looking for what came of a period finds it in the same place in every entry.

entities.name: Sharing
entities.tagline: What was learned, handed to people outside the work — a talk, a written case, a session taught.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
An achievement whose claim is that people outside the work now know something: a conference talk, a published case, a workshop for another team. The audience is the point of the bullet and the bullet names it.

Explaining a decision to the people who had to accept it is part of Decisions, not this. A talk about work done elsewhere is this kind even when the entry exists only for the talk.

entities.name: Billing period
entities.tagline: The stretch of time one invoice charges for, set by the contract, with a first and a last day.

entities.name: Contract
entities.tagline: The terms a customer agreed to buy under, in the words both sides signed, from the day they take effect until they are replaced or ended.

entities.name: Credit note
entities.tagline: A document that lowers what a customer owes on an invoice already issued, leaving that invoice as it was.

entities.name: Customer
entities.tagline: A person or company that has agreed to a contract or pays under one — the party an invoice is addressed to, never the company that issues it.

entities.name: Invoice
entities.tagline: What one customer is asked to pay for one billing period, as a document that stays as it was issued.

entities.name: Invoice line
entities.tagline: One charge on an invoice: an amount, and the reason for that amount in terms the customer agreed to.

entities.name: Pricing rule
entities.tagline: One term of a contract in a form that can be applied: what it charges for, at what price and under which conditions, named as the contract names it.

entities.name: Usage record
entities.tagline: One thing a customer used that a contract charges for — a call made, a seat held, a gigabyte stored — with when it happened and how much of it there was.

entities.name: Invoicing
entities.tagline: What a customer is asked to pay, for which period and on which document, and how a document already issued is corrected. What a term of a contract means, and the amount it produces, is left to Pricing.

entities.name: Pricing
entities.tagline: What a customer agreed to pay for, and how each term of that agreement turns what they used into an amount. Which invoice an amount lands on, and when it is issued, is left to Invoicing.

entities.name: Community
entities.tagline: Work done in public — a talk, a seat, a working group, a published case.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
A period whose output is addressed to people outside the organization paying for it: a conference talk, a board or committee seat, a standards or user group, a case study published under someone else's name. `organization` names the host — the conference, the group, the publisher — not an employer.

A one-off writes `end` equal to `start`; a seat held over years does not. Both are this kind: what makes it community work is the audience, not the duration.

entities.name: Education
entities.tagline: A degree, a certification, a course.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
A period whose output is a qualification rather than a delivery. `organization` names the awarding body — the school, the certifying institute — which is the one case where the field does not name somewhere work was done.

Learning that happened during a role is not this kind. Every role teaches something; what makes a period education is that the qualification is the point of it.

entities.name: Project
entities.tagline: A delivery worth naming on its own, inside a role or beside one.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
A period defined by what it produced rather than by who it was spent with: a system, a migration, a launch. Client work and internal work alike. `organization` names the client, or the organization the work was done for when that differs from the employer.

It ends when the delivery does. A project that has no end and no deliverable is a role described by its current work.

entities.name: Role
entities.tagline: A position held in an organization — the employment history.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
A period spent working for an organization under an arrangement that outlasts any one piece of work: employment, a long-running contract, a partnership. `organization` names the employer.

It is not a delivery. What was built during a role belongs to a project, and a role that lists one delivery in its achievements is usually two periods written as one. The test is whether the period would have continued had the work changed: if it would, it is a role.

entities.name: Billing run
entities.tagline: A finance team can close a billing period and have every invoice for it issued at once, the same whoever runs it.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: Closing a period applies every contract’s rules to the usage recorded in it and issues one invoice per customer, and running it twice on the same inputs issues the same invoices. It ends when the invoices are issued. Sending reminders and collecting payment come after it and are not part of it.

entities.name: Charge explanation
entities.tagline: Anyone reading an invoice can tell how each charge was reached, in the words of the contract they agreed to.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: Every line on an invoice carries the term of the contract that produced it and the usage that term was applied to, and the explanation beside the line is rendered from both. The person paying reads it where they read the invoice, and the finance team that issued it reads the same words when a question reaches them. It explains the arithmetic and stops there: whether the contract says what the payer believes it says is a question for the contract, and nothing here answers it.

entities.name: Credit notes
entities.tagline: A finance team can correct an invoice already sent, and the payer can read what changed and why.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: A credit note is issued against an invoice when the usage it read or the rule it applied turns out wrong, and it is computed from the corrected usage or the corrected rule, so every line on it explains itself the way an invoice line does. It never changes the invoice it corrects, and it carries no amount typed in by hand.

entities.name: Invoice download
entities.tagline: Whoever pays an invoice can keep a copy of it in their own books, exactly as it was issued.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: The copy is a file holding the invoice as issued, with every line and its explanation, and it matches what the page shows on the day it was issued and on every day after. It is a copy and nothing more: paying, disputing and asking a question about the invoice happen elsewhere.

entities.name: Pricing rules
entities.tagline: A finance team can write each term of a contract as a rule every billing run applies, named as the contract names it.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: A rule states what a term charges for, at what price and under which conditions, and it belongs to the contract it was written from, so a new version of the contract brings new versions of its rules. It records prices and never proposes them. A term the rules cannot express is not approximated: the term is renegotiated or the rules grow, and until one of those happens the term is not billed.

entities.name: Usage reporting
entities.tagline: Usage can be reported by the systems that see it happen, as it happens, so nobody types it in at the end of the month.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: Each report becomes a usage record under the contract it counts against, kept as it was sent. It records and does not correct: a report sent wrong is answered by a second report that offsets it, never by editing the first, so what a billing run read can always be read again.

entities.name: Beacon Systems
entities.tagline: Billing software for companies whose pricing outgrew their spreadsheets.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
We build and run the billing platform our customers invoice their own customers through. Two teams, one platform, and a domain we are still splitting into the shapes it wants to be in.

We sell to companies at the point where pricing has become a system rather than a page — usage, tiers, credits, corrections — and where getting an invoice wrong costs more than the invoice.

entities.name: Delivery
entities.tagline: How a change to the platform is specified, built and released.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never begins a phase whose predecessor's gate has not been approved.
- Never releases a change that no reviewer has read.
- Never counts a check nobody ran as a check that passed.

entities.name: Build
entities.tagline: Make the change and have it read, one track at a time.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: An approved specification, and a branch off the platform's main line.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
### Code

1. Write the failing test, then the change that passes it.
2. Hand the diff to the Reviewer with the specification beside it.
3. Resolve every finding, or record why it stands.

### Docs

1. Draft the page from the specification.
2. Have the Reviewer read it against what the change actually does.

rows: Commits on a branch, with the suite passing and every finding resolved
The customer-facing description of what changed, unpublished
Commits on a branch, with the suite passing and every finding resolved
The customer-facing description of what changed, unpublished

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never changes a test's expectation to make it pass.
- Never publishes the page before the change is released.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Build, all of these hold:

- The suite passes on the branch.
- Every review finding is resolved or recorded with a reason.
- The branch does what the specification said, and nothing else.

Where they cannot be met, the Reviewer decides whether the branch is reworked or abandoned.

entities.name: Release
entities.tagline: Put the change in front of the platform's users, and the page with it.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A branch that left Build, and the draft page written beside it.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. Merge the branch and tag the release.
2. Publish the page.
3. Watch the platform until the change has been exercised by real traffic.

rows: Merged, tagged, and running for users
The page describing the change, live on the customer site
Merged, tagged, and running for users
The page describing the change, live on the customer site

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never releases and publishes in the opposite order.
- Never leaves a release untagged.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
Release is the last phase. The work is done when all of these hold:

- The change is merged and tagged.
- The page is live.
- The change has been exercised in production without incident.

Where they cannot be met, the Reviewer decides whether the release is rolled back.

entities.name: Specify
entities.tagline: Write down what the change must do, before anyone writes how it does it.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A request from the platform's users, and the part of the system it will touch, read rather than remembered.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. State the request as one sentence.
2. Name the approaches worth considering, and recommend one.
3. Write down what the change must do, and what it is explicitly not doing.

rows: What the change must do, the approach chosen, and what was left out
What the change must do, the approach chosen, and what was left out

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never writes the change it specifies.
- Never leaves a question unasked because an assumption would be convenient.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Specify, all of these hold:

- The request is stated as one sentence.
- The approach is chosen and the rejected ones are named.
- What the change will not do is written down.

Where they cannot be met, the Reviewer decides whether the request is reshaped or dropped.

entities.name: Code
entities.tagline: A merged change to the platform.

entities.name: Docs
entities.tagline: A published page on the customer site.

entities.name: Billing Console
entities.tagline: The web application where the finance team of a company billing through Beacon keeps its pricing, runs its billing and answers for every invoice that goes out.

entities.name: Invoice Page
entities.tagline: The page every invoice links to, opened by whoever has to pay it.

entities.name: Usage API
entities.tagline: The interface the systems of a company billing through Beacon send usage to, set up by the developers who connect them.

entities.name: Competent
entities.tagline: Reliable alone. Unsupervised work with a predictable result.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text: Someone at this level works with it unsupervised and the result is predictable. They recognize the common failure modes, having run into them.

entities.name: Expert
entities.tagline: Knows the limits. Has worked below the surface, shaped it, or taught it.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text: Someone at this level knows where it breaks down and where it is simply wrong. They have worked below its surface, shaped it, or taught it.

entities.name: Familiar
entities.tagline: Needs support. Real use, with guidance or frequent reference.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text: Someone at this level has used it on real work, with guidance or frequent reference. They can follow a conversation about it and make sense of other people's work in it.

entities.name: Proficient
entities.tagline: Exercises judgment. Chooses between alternatives and can say why.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text: Someone at this level makes judgment calls in it and can explain why the alternatives are worse. Other people bring them their questions.

entities.name: AI Agent
entities.tagline: Whichever agent reviews a change at Beacon Systems today, held to the same seat whichever model it is.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: One profile for every agent the company runs, so the seat has a holder. It claims no skill, and not because the first review is unread: a claim is a person's history with a capability, and an agent has none. What holds it to the seat is the rulebook, never a row.

entities.name: Backend Engineer
entities.tagline: The seat that keeps the services the product runs on correct, and answers for them when they are not.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A bounded context with a name and the invoices it has to get right. A change request that says what is wrong for a customer, not which class to edit. A turn on the pager, because the seat answers for what it ships.

sections.heading: What it produces
sections.text: A service that stays up, and a change small enough that a reviewer reads it in one sitting, with the tests that show the invoice is still right.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never merges its own change.
- Never moves a seam between contexts on its own; where a seam sits is the domain's decision.
- Never ships a change the invoice tests do not cover.

entities.name: Reviewer
entities.tagline: The seat that reads one change against what was asked, returns findings with a severity and changes nothing.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: The change as a diff, the request it answers and the report of whoever made it, read as a claim rather than a fact.

sections.heading: What it produces
sections.text: Findings, each with a file, a line, what is wrong, why it matters and how to fix it, ranked by severity, and the strengths named first. A finding is an input to whoever merges.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never edits the change it reviews.
- Never re-runs a suite to confirm a report; it runs one focused test on a doubt the report
  does not answer.
- Never calls polish critical.

entities.name: Domain-Driven Design
entities.tagline: Modeling software around the language the business already speaks.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Name things as the business names them, and refuse a name that only makes sense inside the codebase. Draw the boundary between one model and the next, and hold it when a second team wants to reach across it. Rework the model when the language changes, rather than mapping around it and keeping both.

entities.name: Java Programming
entities.tagline: Building and maintaining server-side systems on the JVM.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Write services other teams depend on, and keep them running once they do. Read the stack trace when one stops. Know the runtime well enough to tell a slow query from a slow collector, and to say which of the two a graph is showing. Typical tools: the JDK, a build tool, a profiler.

entities.name: Product Discovery
entities.tagline: Finding out what is worth building before building it.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Talk to the people who would use a thing before the first line of it is written. Frame the question so that the answer can be no, and hear it when it is. Test the cheapest version of an idea that could still turn out wrong, and stop when it does.

entities.name: Google Workspace
entities.tagline: The company's directory and documents; people and groups are synced from here. A `source-id` is the directory's user id.

entities.name: Local
entities.tagline: Written and kept in this repository; nothing syncs it.

entities.name: Support stops explaining invoices
entities.tagline: A customer who opens an invoice gets the same explanation support would have given, without the call.

sections.heading: What it makes true
sections.text:
A customer looking at an invoice can tell how each number was reached, in the words their own contract uses, so the question "why is this line 4,200" is answered where it is asked. Support still hears from customers, and what it hears about is their pricing rather than our arithmetic.

We would know it holds by what stops arriving. An explanation ticket is one where the customer asks how a number was reached and nothing about the number is wrong; those are countable today and they are the measure. The invoice being correct is not what is in question and never was.

What falls outside: a disagreement about what the contract says. An invoice that explains itself perfectly can still bill something the customer believes they did not buy, and that is a question for the contract, not for the page.

entities.name: Invoicing Strategy
entities.tagline: The invoice is rendered from the pricing rules themselves, so its explanation is generated rather than written.

sections.heading: The approach
sections.text:
We keep the pricing rules as data the billing run reads, rather than code it executes: one rule per pricing term, named in the words the contract uses, versioned with the contract it belongs to. A line on an invoice carries the id of the rule that produced it, and the explanation a customer reads is rendered from that rule and the inputs it saw. One run produces both the number and the sentence about the number, which is what keeps them from drifting apart.

Where a rule cannot express a term, we renegotiate the term or we grow the rule language. Neither is quick, and choosing that over a manual adjustment is the whole of this strategy.

sections.heading: What it rules out
sections.text: We never add a manual adjustment line. An invoice that anyone can add a number to is an invoice that cannot explain itself, and every exception granted teaches the next team to ask for one. We never write the explanation by hand after the fact, however well written it would be: a sentence maintained beside a number is a second copy of a rule, and it goes stale on the first pricing change nobody remembers to follow. And we keep no per-customer pricing code, which is the fast way to win one deal and the slow way to lose the ability to explain anything.

sections.heading: What would show it is working
sections.text: We watch the share of invoice lines whose rule id is missing, which is countable on every run and should fall to nothing. Then the share of explanation tickets in support's queue, which moves later and is read monthly. The first number moves within a sprint of any pricing change, which is what makes it worth watching — by the time the second one moves, the change that broke it is months old.

entities.name: Beacon Systems website
entities.tagline: The company's own site, where a buyer who has heard the name lands first, rebuilt from the model on every change.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text:
- **Home** — the identity's tagline and `## What it is`.
- **Principles** — the vision and the values.
- **Team** — the profiles, each with the roles it holds.
- **How we deliver** — the process and its phases, in order.

entities.name: Partner directory
entities.tagline: The listing a buyer reaches from the directory's search, maintained by hand because the directory takes no feed.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text:
- **Company name and one-line description** — the identity's H1 and its tagline, unchanged.
- **The long description** — the identity's `## What it is`, cut to the directory's limit.
- **Capabilities** — the skills held at Proficient or Expert, under their own names.
- **Contact** — the identity's `email` and `url`.

sections.heading: Projection rules
sections.text:
- The long description is the identity's `## What it is` up to the limit below, cut at a
  paragraph and never mid-sentence. Nothing is written for the directory that is not in the
  model first.
- Capabilities carry no proficiency level. The directory shows a flat list and a level beside
  a name it does not explain reads as a grade, so the level decides which skills appear rather
  than appearing itself.
- Skills held at Familiar or Competent are left out. The listing is what the company sells, and
  a capability still being learned is not.
- No profile is named. The directory lists companies, and a person named here would be a fact
  about the company that the company's own identity does not carry.

sections.heading: Constraints
sections.text:
- The long description is at most 600 characters, the directory's limit, read from its editor
  on 2026-01-05.
- Every capability named is a skill in the model, spelled as that skill's H1.
- The contact address resolves to the company and not to a person.

entities.name: Craftsmanship
entities.tagline: We would rather ship one thing that holds up than three that need watching.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
We refuse a deadline that can only be met by leaving something half-built, and we say so early enough that the date can still move.

We never ship on time while knowing privately which part will be rewritten within the quarter.

entities.name: Say The Hard Thing
entities.tagline: Disagreement that arrives after the decision is not disagreement, it is commentary.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
We name the objection in the room where the choice is being made, once and plainly, and then commit to whatever is decided.

We never agree in the meeting and reopen the question in a side channel afterwards.

entities.name: Billing nobody has to explain
entities.tagline: A customer reading one of our invoices can tell how the number was reached, without calling us and without a spreadsheet beside it.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
Every charge traces to something the customer did, in language they used when they agreed to it. When an invoice is disputed the answer is in the invoice, and support confirms it rather than reconstructing it. We would know this holds when disputes are resolved by reading rather than by investigation.

It says nothing about what we charge or whom we sell to. Pricing models and market are decisions we expect to change several times; this is what we want to be true of the bill whatever they turn out to be.
